proposals.subject: Florida manatee
proposals.title: Her turn
proposals.content: My calf put her nose against my side and pushed. I hardly moved. She tried again, harder. This time I turned a little with her. We went round in a slow circle, her tail working furiously. She let go looking very pleased. I waited until she was beside me before going the way I had meant to go.
proposals.review: Nellie is the larger mother at left. FWS title identifies mother and calf, exact setting Three Sisters Springs matches Crystal River. Nose-to-side contact is visible. Repeated pushing, circular movement and mutual feelings are fictional. Introduces adult motherhood explicitly, no age reset. The calf is a fictional daughter; the source does not determine calf sex. Physical accommodation becomes deliberate encouragement; no crowd-fit or warm-water joke.

proposals.subject: California sea lion
proposals.title: Go round again
proposals.content: When we were young, I put the kelp between us because he kept coming too close. He went around it. I turned with the stalk. By the third time I was waiting for him to try the other side.
proposals.review: Explicit younger memory, placed after the childhood itch and before adult motherhood. Foreground small slender sea lion, extended flipper, intervening kelp and nearby companions support the bodily game. Circling and change from discomfort to anticipation are fiction, not observed sequence. Source names California sea lion and Channel Islands location. No mature male crest visible; source does not prove sex, so no claim that photographer sexed this animal. Preserve exact named photographer credit and explicit asset-level Public domain / Full record.

proposals.subject: Florida manatee
proposals.title: Remembering the first bite
proposals.content: Showed her how to pull up the grass. She got a mouthful of sand and came back under my flipper for milk. I went over the patch again while she drank. There was sand in mine too. I had forgotten that part.
proposals.review: Nursing image is biologically suitable and explicit public-domain. The grass encounter and recognition are fiction outside frame. Hold: still a feeding-mishap mechanism, and the child sex would need an explicit fictional decision. Do not append or count. No nursing absence or forced weaning invented.

sourceReview.sourceCaption: During Dive 04 of the Papahānaumokuākea ROV and Mapping expedition, at a depth of 1,532 meters (5,026 feet), this brittle star was observed with its arms deeply entwined around the branches of a  Metallagorgia  sp. coral. sourceReview.sourceCaption:
Towards the end of Dive 11 of the 2021 North Atlantic Stepping Stones expedition, we moved from stable ripples and pavement to softer sediments with smaller fractions of broken paleo reef. The seafloor here was pockmarked with circular patches of turned-over sediments, and we also observed larger scar marks that were likely feeding holds for fish and/or Chaceon crabs — like the one pictured here.

sourceReview.sourceCaption: A stare down with this octopus (Mussoctopus sp.), occurred during Dive 08 of the Seascape Alaska 5 expedition. As we observed it, the octopus displayed its abilities to change color using specialized cells in its skin called chromatophores. It flashed the deep reddish purple seen here before turning completely white within seconds.
